headline: Hadaka was originally 肌 (hada, “skin”) plus 赤 (aka, “red”).
Isamashii is 勇む (isamu) plus しい (-shii).
Mi is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Ritsu, “rate”, is from Middle Chinese 率 (MC lwit).
Buki is from Middle Chinese 武器 (MC mjuX khijH).
Tabemono is tabe, the stem of 食べる (taberu, “to eat”), plus 物 (-mono, “thing”).
Hakari is the continuative stem of 量る (hakaru).
Kenkyūshitsu is 研究 (kenkyū, “research”) plus 室 (-shitsu, “room”).
Hanko comes from 版行 (hankō) > hanko.
Kumiai went from kumiapi through kumiaɸi and kumiawi to kumiai.
Itsumo is いつ (itsu, “when”) plus も (mo, “even, also”).
Kuyamu is derived from 悔いる (kuiru).
Ateru is from Old Japanese 当つ (atu), in the lower bigrade pattern.
Kōkō contracts 高等学校 (kōtō-gakkō, “high school”).
Kiri is the continuative stem of 切る (kiru, “to cut”).
Satsu, “bill”, is from Middle Chinese 札 (MC tsreat).
Shōbōsho is 消防 (shōbō, “fire fighting”) plus 署 (-sho, “station, office”).
Otoru is cognate with 落ちる (ochiru, “to fall”), via an Old Japanese root ot-.
Utsuru, “to move”, is cognate with 写る.
Issakujitsu is 一昨 (issaku-, “the previous... before...”) plus 日 (jitsu, “day”), first cited to a text from 1275.
Sakari is the continuative stem of 盛る (sakaru).
Mazui is derived from 貧しい (mazushii, “poor”).
Ine is attested in the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE, and is possibly related to 米 (yone).
Taisen is 大 (tai, “big, large”) plus 戦 (sen, “battle”).
Tachiba is compared on its page to English standpoint.
Tsugu, “to pour”, is cognate with 継ぐ (tsugu).
Manabu is 真似 (mana, “imitating, copying”) plus ぶ (-bu, “to seem like, to act like”): “to learn” as “to imitate”.
Motomeru is from the Classical Japanese verb 求む (motomu).
Kandenchi is 乾 (kan) plus 電池 (denchi).
Ōjo is Middle Chinese 王女, literally “king + female”, the kan'on reading.
Hori is the continuative stem of 掘る (horu, “to dig”).
